terms.gloss: be snowed under, overwhelmed (with work, business)
terms.grammar: passive infinitive of obruō, obruere, obruī, obrutum, with the ablative of what buries one
evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 1.1.4: nēve tē obruī tamquam flūctū, sīc magnitūdine negōtiī sinās (Lewis & Short s.v. tamquam)
Traupman 105: to be overwhelmed with work, obruī, tamquam flūctū, sīc opere
terms.comment: Literally “to be buried, overwhelmed”: Latin says what one is buried under in the ablative, negōtiīs obruī. Cicero adds the image of a wave, tamquam fluctū, which Traupman keeps.

sources: Lewis & Short: obruo
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 105, 108, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
